title: What a map decides — Image Wiki
text:
What a map decides
  Everything on a map matters to somebody and it all has to fit in one plane. Five principles decide what wins — and the first real decision is which question the map is for.

  
    Termcartographic design principles / map hierarchy
    Also calledmap design principles, figure-ground on maps, cartographic hierarchy, generalisation
    Not the same asmap projection, map accuracy, GIS analysis
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Esri's five, as decisionsA map is designed against a questionThe same map cannot serve every taskCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Pull the tourist map out of a hotel drawer and try to answer one question: which way is the station. The answer is on the sheet. So is every hotel, every one-way arrow, every park, three typefaces, a boat-trip advertisement, and a grid of letters down the margin. The map has your answer and will not hand it over.
That is the standing problem, and it is harder than it looks because of one asymmetry. A chart has a variable or two and a lot of white paper. A map has coastline, relief, roads, rail, rivers, boundaries, place names, land use and your data — all of it real, all of it wanted by somebody, all of it competing for the same square centimetre. There is no second page.
Esri's five, as decisions
Esri's set is the one everything else in cartography assumes: legibility, visual contrast, figure-ground, hierarchy, balance. The first two are what makes the content visible at all; the last three lead the reader through it. Each is a question with an answer you have to write down.
Legibility — what must survive the smallest size this will be seen at? Esri's definition is "the ability to be seen and understood", and both halves bite. A shape can be big enough to see and still mean nothing. Their practical rule: geometric symbols stay readable when small, complex ones need room. Mapbox puts a hard floor on the same idea — a point-of-interest icon has to work at 11px. Decide the smallest intended size first, then design at it, not at 200%.
Visual contrast — where are you spending it? Contrast is finite in the sense that matters: if everything is emphatic, nothing is. Esri's analogy is a dark room, where too little reflected light leaves you unable to separate one object from another. Turn contrast up and features separate; turn it down and they read as belonging together, which is precisely why a basemap should be low-contrast. Two consequences worth remembering: what stands out is usually whatever is darker or brighter, and low contrast is a tool rather than a failure. See Contrast.
Figure-ground — what is the subject, and what is the surroundings? Gestalt gave us the words: the spontaneous separation of a figure with a definite contour from a background with none. Esri lists the moves — show the area of interest as a closed form, wash the surround out, add a drop shadow, feather the edge, screen it back, vignette it.

area of interestOne visual planeevery road the same weight — nothing is the subjectFigure separated from groundsame lines, same places; the surround screened back

Identical geometry in both panels: the same four roads, the same river, the same lake, the same five settlements, the same dashed boundary. One thing changes.
Left, every line is drawn at the same weight, so the dashed boundary is just another line and your eye has nowhere to start. Right, one veil of the page colour lies over everything outside the boundary. Nothing was deleted and nothing was thickened — the surround simply lost contrast, and the district came forward. That is the whole trick.


Hierarchy — what recedes, and what goes entirely? Esri splits this by map type. On a reference map most features deserve roughly the same visual plane, and the order is often physical: physiography at the bottom, then water, vegetation, human-made features, then boundaries. On a thematic map the base recedes so the theme can climb above it, and Mapbox's version of the same rule is that base content is kept to a minimum. In both, labels sit on the highest plane, because a label nobody can read is not information. This is Visual hierarchy with a much longer queue of contenders.



Ordnance Survey One-Inch Sheet 90, Wensleydale, published 1961. Crown copyright expired; public domain. Click to enlarge.
A reference map with no single subject, so the hierarchy has to be subtle enough that a reader can pick their own. Six layers, from the back forward: a pale buff ground tint carrying thin orange contours; blue water; green woodland; the road network in red and yellow; black for buildings, tracks and symbols; and black type above everything.
The contours are the tell. They cover every square inch, they are the densest feature on the sheet, and they still lose — because they are drawn thin and pale, so the roads cross them without a fight. Squint and the red road along Wensleydale is the first thing you see. Nothing was deleted to achieve that.


Balance — is the weight distributed on purpose? Esri describes the page as balancing on a fulcrum, tipped by the position, size, shape and subject of everything on it, and notes a useful specific: the visual centre sits slightly above the geometric centre. Their two posts disagree on the name — the earlier one calls the fifth principle balance, the later one folds balance inside proportion alongside symmetry and harmony. The names differ; the checks do not.
A map is designed against a question
The British Cartographic Society's design group put this first, in 1999, and bluntly: concept before compilation — "a map without a purpose is of no use to anyone." Their next two are the ones people skip. Hierarchy with harmony: important things prominent, the rest fading back. Simplicity from sacrifice: "a map can be considered complete when no other features can be removed."



John Snow, map of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak; lithograph by C. F. Cheffins, London. Public domain. Commons dates this file to 1854; the sheet is headed Map 1, as it appeared in the 1855 second edition.
One question: where were the deaths, relative to the pumps? Everything on the sheet serves it and nothing else does. Deaths are stacked black bars at their addresses, so a bad house reads as a thick block. Pumps are dots labelled PUMP in the only bold word on the map. Buildings are hairline outlines with no fill, no relief, no land use, no tint.
Look at Broad Street, centre: a wall of black. Now look at the workhouse to the north-west and Golden Square to the south — big, populous, and almost blank. That contrast is the argument, and it is visible in about a second because Snow threw everything else away.


Dropping things entirely is the move people find hardest, so here is a map that drops almost everything.



Admiralty Chart No. 2491, New York Harbour, United Kingdom Hydrographic Office, published 1857, corrected to 1867. Public domain.
Figure-ground, inverted on purpose. The water is the figure — thousands of engraved soundings, shoals, channels, the Sandy Hook bar. Manhattan and Brooklyn are the ground: a faint scribble of streets, unlabelled, with Long Island trailing off as a ghost. A city of several hundred thousand people has been reduced to the shape of an obstacle.
Note the extras that follow from the question. A table of lights top left. Coastal profile views along the bottom margin, drawn as the land looks from the sea at a stated bearing, because that is how you find the entrance. Useless for finding a hotel. Correct for not sinking.


The same map cannot serve every task


What rock is under here: Smith, 1815
How do I get there: Cary, 1794


Left: William Smith, A Delineation of the Strata of England and Wales, with part of Scotland, 1815. Right: John Cary, Cary's New Map of England and Wales, with part of Scotland, 1794 (composite of the sheets). Both public domain.
The same island at almost the same date, drawn against different questions, and you can see which is which from across the room. On Smith's map the figure is colour: bands of strata sweeping south-east, with towns and roads ghosted underneath as thin grey. On Cary's, colour barely appears and the figure is the black mesh of post roads and place names; there is no geology at all, because a coach driver does not care.
Neither map answers the other's question. That is not a limitation of 18th-century printing — it is the choice being made properly.


The failure mode is refusing to choose. A map that tries to answer every question ends up with nine layers on one visual plane, and answers all of them slowly. The related failure is a map answering a question nobody asked: raw counts shaded by area are a population map wearing a costume, which is the map version of the problem in How accurately a chart can be read.
Common mistakes

"I'll decide what to cut once it looks crowded." Backwards. Decide the question, then admit only what serves it. Otherwise everything you already drew feels earned.
"Turning the important layer up will fix it." Only if something else comes down. Emphasis is relative, and both Esri and Mapbox say the same thing: the principles are complementary, not applied one at a time.
"A reference map has no hierarchy." It has a subtle one, and a deliberate one. Esri's point is that its features share a plane so the reader can pick their own subject — which only works if the labels stay above everything.
"More detail is more honest." Campbell and Shin cite Monmonier's How to Lie with Maps for the opposite: maps distort as readily as statistics, and clutter is one of the ways.


Reading a map in five seconds

Say the one question this map is for. If you cannot, that is the finding.
What is the figure? What is doing the work of being ground?
Find the smallest text and smallest symbol. Legible here, at this size?
Where is the contrast spent — on the theme, or on the base?
Name one thing that should have been dropped, and one thing that is missing.

              Difference — how much a part of a picture differs from what sits next to it. An edge exists only where something changes, so contrast is what makes anything visible at all.
